name: Qing China
title: Social Hierarchy of Qing China: From Emperor to Bondservants

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You rule as Son of Heaven and absolute master of the Boards, decide every great matter with your Grand Council in the Inner Court, and are khan to the Mongols and patron of Tibetan Buddhism.
tiers.kid: The emperor ruled China and the lands beyond it from the Forbidden City in Beijing.
tiers.rise: The throne passed among the sons of the imperial house: on the Kangxi Emperor’s death in 1722 his fourth son became the Yongzheng Emperor, and in 1735 Yongzheng’s son became the Qianlong Emperor. A child emperor reigned through regents, as Kangxi did from the age of seven.
tiers.why: The emperor was an absolute ruler who presided over the six Boards and held, in Confucian theory, the Mandate of Heaven.

tiers.name: The imperial clan and the Manchu nobility
tiers.term: Aisin Gioro (the imperial house), the Eight Great Houses, qinwang (prince of the blood)
tiers.you: You are a prince of the imperial house: you may command a banner, sit in the Inner Court and marry your daughters into the families of generals, but the emperor watches every prince who might threaten the throne.
tiers.kid: Princes of the emperor’s family and a few great Manchu families held noble titles and led the banner armies.
tiers.rise: Noble rank came by birth or by the emperor’s grant, and the father and brothers of an emperor’s mother were raised into the Upper Three Manchu Banners. Rank could be lost as quickly: after his death in 1650 Dorgon was stripped of his titles and his family and associates purged.
tiers.why: Above the officials stood a small hereditary aristocracy: the princes of the imperial Aisin Gioro house and the Manchu nobles of the “Eight Great Houses”, who held noble titles, as against the commoner bannermen (irgen).

tiers.name: Officials
tiers.you: You passed the palace examination and now govern a county far from your home, judging cases and collecting the land tax on a salary so small that you live on irregular fees.
tiers.kid: Officials who had passed very hard exams ran the government, from ministers in Beijing to the judges of every county.
tiers.rise: Office came chiefly through the examinations: graduates of the metropolitan examination were assured influential posts, but qualified men so far exceeded the vacancies that many waited years, and purchase of office became common in the 19th century. Appointments ran for three years, with an evaluation at the end, and Qianlong’s son forced Heshen to commit suicide.
tiers.why: The Qing kept the Ming bureaucracy and divided its posts into civil and military, each in nine grades, from a Grand Secretary down to a deputy jail warden.

tiers.name: The degree-holding gentry
tiers.term: shengyuan or xiucai, juren, jinshi (the degrees)
tiers.you: You have passed the first examinations and wear the robes of a shengyuan: you owe no labour service, speak to the magistrate as an equal, and teach village boys while you study for the provincial examination.
tiers.kid: Men who passed the first exams became gentry, the leaders of their towns and villages.
tiers.rise: Any commoner of good status could sit the examinations, but years of study, travel and gifts to examiners made a candidate the burden of his whole family, and in the Ming and Qing only about one candidate in a hundred passed the provincial examination. Merchant families could also buy degrees.
tiers.why: The gentry were defined by law: a man who had passed at least the first level of the examinations held a degree that qualified him for office, and his wife and some relatives shared his status.

tiers.name: Bannermen
tiers.term: jakūn gūsa (the Eight Banners), irgen (commoner bannermen)
tiers.you: You were born into a banner company and draw a stipend and grain from the state in a garrison quarter; banner courts judge you, and marrying a civilian woman can bring you punishment.
tiers.kid: Bannermen were soldier families, many of them Manchu, who were paid by the emperor and lived in their own quarters of the cities.
tiers.rise: Banner status was inherited. Han Chinese entered by adoption into Manchu households, often for money, and were registered apart as “separate-register” bannermen; deserters from destitute garrisons were sentenced to penal slavery or death.
tiers.why: Every Manchu household belonged to one of the Eight Banners, which had been joined by Mongol and Han Chinese banners: in effect twenty-four armies, in companies of nominally 300 men.

tiers.name: Buddhist, Daoist and other clergy
tiers.you: You are a monk of a Tibetan Buddhist temple in Beijing, built by the emperor, and the magistrates watch to see that your teaching stays within the bounds the state allows.
tiers.kid: Monks and priests looked after temples, and the emperor himself built great Buddhist temples in Beijing.
tiers.rise: Entering a monastery or temple took a man or woman out of the four occupations; the state could also close the door, as when the Yongzheng Emperor outlawed Christianity in 1723 and expelled most of the missionaries.
tiers.why: The clergy stood outside the four occupations.

tiers.name: Farmers
tiers.you: You farm a few acres with your family, pay your rent in silver and sell part of the crop in the market town, while the village grows faster than its land.
tiers.kid: Most people were farmers, and new crops such as sweet potatoes and peanuts helped feed a fast-growing population.
tiers.rise: A prospering farm family could educate a son for the examinations, the road to the gentry, though the cost fell on the whole family. Millions moved instead, to Yunnan, Guizhou, Taiwan and the highlands, and poverty drove some families to sell children under the guise of adoption.
tiers.why: In the Confucian scheme farmers stood second, after the scholars, as the primary creators of wealth, and Qing law counted them among the good people.

tiers.name: Artisans
tiers.you: You work for wages under a master in a small weaving workshop, and your trade’s guild hall sets the rules and the prices.
tiers.kid: Craftspeople made silk, paper and fine porcelain, and some of it was shipped all the way to Europe.
tiers.rise: Artisans were good people, so a prosperous craftsman’s family, like any family of good status, could try to put a son through the examinations.
tiers.why: Artisans came third in the four occupations, makers of useful things, and Qing law counted them among the good people.

tiers.name: Merchants
tiers.you: You are a salt merchant of Yangzhou, rich enough to patronise poets and actors, and you have paid for tutors so that your son may pass the examinations.
tiers.kid: Merchants were placed last in old Chinese ideas, but many grew rich trading salt, tea and silk.
tiers.rise: Merchants could buy degrees, and under the Ming and Qing their sons could sit the examinations: in 1711 the success of salt merchants’ sons at Yangzhou led to a bribery case and the chief examiner’s execution. By the late imperial period gentry and merchant families overlapped and mixed.
tiers.why: Merchants stood last in Confucian theory, seen as a social disturbance for piling up wealth, but Qing law counted them among the good people, and many were far richer than their place suggested.

tiers.name: Banner bondservants
tiers.term: booi aha (booi niyalma, men, booi hehe, women), aha
tiers.you: You were born into a bondservant household of one of the Upper Three Banners and serve in the Imperial Household Department, managing silk workshops in Jiangnan for the emperor’s household, which your family serves by inheritance.
tiers.kid: Bondservant families served a banner household for generations; some farmed, while others ran the emperor’s palace business.
tiers.rise: The status was inherited, but booi families could be moved into the Manchu banners by the emperor’s order, and Manchu families adopted bondservants’ sons, often for payment; the court discovered such adoptions in 1729, and their descendants came to fill soldiers’ places in the banners.
tiers.why: The booi aha, “household people”, were hereditarily servile members of the banners, often translated “bondservants”.

tiers.name: The mean people
tiers.you: You act in an opera troupe: the crowds applaud you, but the law counts you among the mean people, forbids you the examinations and expects you to bow to commoners.
tiers.kid: Actors, entertainers and some poor workers were called “mean people” by law and were not allowed to take the exams.
tiers.rise: Mean status closed the road of the examinations. The emperor, his court and the bureaucracy worked to reduce the distinction between the debased and the free, but even at the end of the dynasty they had not merged the two.
tiers.why: Below the good people Qing law placed the mean people: entertainers, including actors and prostitutes, tattooed criminals and the low-level employees of government officials; the rules of the examinations also name…

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: After a revolt in the northwest was crushed, you were exiled across the empire to serve as a slave in the household of a banner officer at Guangzhou.
tiers.kid: Some people were enslaved, often as a punishment for crimes, even though one emperor tried to end slavery.
tiers.rise: People fell into slavery by a criminal sentence, by the sale of poor families’ children, or as rebels and deserters punished by the state; the Yongzheng Emperor’s attempt to abolish slavery did not succeed.
tiers.why: Slavery was comparatively uncommon in Chinese history and was practised largely as a judicial punishment.
